name: Paolo Banchero
notes: Duke's ACC Rookie of the Year and consensus Second-Team All-American (17.2/7.8/3.2), an unusually complete, do-everything scoring forward from a single dominant freshman season. Orlando took him 1st. Banchero delivered instantly (27 points on debut, the first since LeBron with 25/5/5 in a debut), won Rookie of the Year, made his first All-Star team in 2024 and posted a first career triple-double, then a 50-point game in 2025 before a torn oblique cost him time; he signed a $239M extension and remains Orlando's franchise cornerstone (22.3/7.4/4.8 career). Hit: exactly the franchise-centerpiece outcome projected for the No. 1 pick.

name: Chet Holmgren
notes: Gonzaga's West Coast Conference Defensive Player and Newcomer of the Year (14.1/9.9/3.7 blk), a true 7-footer with rare perimeter skill and shot-blocking, durability the lone real question given his frame. Oklahoma City took him 2nd. A Lisfranc injury in a pro-am wiped out his entire rookie season, but Holmgren returned in 2023-24 to win All-Rookie First Team honors, then anchored Oklahoma City's 2025 championship (a record five blocks in Finals Game 7) before a first All-Star selection, All-NBA Third Team and All-Defensive First Team in 2025-26. Hit: a true unicorn talent who became a champion and All-Star despite the injury detour.

name: Jabari Smith Jr.
notes: Auburn's USBWA National Freshman of the Year and SEC Freshman of the Year (16.9/7.4/2.0 on 42/42% shooting), a rare big-man shooting profile many projected as a potential No. 1 pick. Houston took him 3rd after Orlando passed. Smith developed into a steady Rockets rotation piece (12.2-12.8 ppg, All-Rookie Second Team) through a fractured hand in January 2025, signing a five-year, $122M extension that June. Solid outcome: real, valuable frontcourt shooting and defense, short of the superstar shooting-big ceiling once projected.

name: Keegan Murray
notes: Iowa's consensus First-Team All-American and Karl Malone Award winner as a sophomore (23.5/8.7 on 55.4/39.8% shooting, a 27-point/21-rebound game), a hyper-efficient, winning-college-production forward. Sacramento took him 4th. Murray won Summer League MVP, then set a rookie record with 206 threes (All-Rookie First Team) and kept scaling up (12.2 to 15.2 to 14.0 ppg), including an 11-consecutive-three, 47-point game in 2023 — signing a $140M extension in 2025 before a torn UCL and later ankle surgery slowed his 2025-26 season. Hit: efficient, winning college production that became a real, valuable NBA starter.

name: Jaden Ivey
notes: Purdue's First-Team All-Big Ten and All-American Second Team sophomore (17.3/4.9/3.1), elite downhill burst and athleticism projected as a top-five talent. Detroit took him 5th. Ivey delivered real scoring (16.3 to 17.6 ppg, All-Rookie Second Team) before a broken fibula and knee surgery limited 2024-25, and a February 2026 trade to Chicago was followed almost immediately by a season-ending knee injury and a waiver for conduct detrimental to the team after controversial social media posts. Bust: real athletic scoring talent whose trajectory was cut short by both injury and an off-court dismissal.

name: Bennedict Mathurin
notes: Arizona's Pac-12 Player of the Year as a sophomore (consensus Second-Team All-American), elite scoring punch and athleticism from a winning program, the first Montreal-born lottery pick. Indiana took him 6th. Mathurin won All-Rookie First Team honors immediately, was 2024 Rising Stars MVP, battled back from a torn labrum requiring surgery, then helped lead Indiana's 2025 Finals run (a 27-point bench outburst in Game 3) before a February 2026 trade to the Clippers (a 38-point home debut). Hit: real, high-level scoring talent and a genuine Finals contributor.

name: Shaedon Sharpe
notes: The consensus No. 1 recruit in his class who never played a college game — Kentucky redshirted him before he declared straight for the draft — pure, unproven physical upside. Portland took him 7th. A shoulder labral tear cost him early development time, but Sharpe developed into a real scorer (9.9 to a 15.9 ppg pace before abdominal surgery, then 18.5/4.5/2.8 in 2024-25), signing a $90M extension in 2025 while playing through a 2026 stress reaction in his fibula. Solid outcome: unusually risky, zero-college-game upside that nonetheless developed into a genuine NBA scorer.

name: Dyson Daniels
notes: A G League Ignite product (12.0/7.1/5.1/2.0 stl) who skipped college entirely, real size-versatility-defense upside on a non-traditional path. New Orleans took him 8th. Daniels's early Pelicans role stayed modest (3.8 to 5.8 ppg) before a 2024 trade to Atlanta unlocked a genuine star turn — an NBA-leading 3.01 steals per game, the first Australian Most Improved Player, All-Defensive First Team in 2025, then a $100M extension and All-Defensive Second Team in 2025-26. Hit: real defensive versatility that became a genuine, statistically historic two-way NBA player.

name: Jeremy Sochan
notes: A one-and-done Baylor big-wing hybrid and Big 12 Sixth Man of the Year (9.2/6.4/1.3 stl), real positional versatility from a title-contending team. San Antonio took him 9th. Sochan settled into a steady four-year Spurs rotation role (9.9/5.4 career, a 33-point game, an unconventional one-handed free throw fix under Gregg Popovich) before a February 2026 waiver, a brief Knicks stint that included a championship-clinching Finals appearance against his former team, and an August 2026 signing with Portland. Solid outcome: a real, versatile NBA rotation player and, briefly, a champion.

name: Johnny Davis
notes: Wisconsin's Big Ten Player of the Year and consensus First-Team All-American as a sophomore (19.7/8.2, a 37-point/14-rebound game, Jerry West and Lute Olson Award winner), elite go-to college scoring. Washington took him 10th. Davis never found NBA footing (112 games, 3.5 ppg, playing time shrinking every season to 7.1 minutes by 2024-25) before a 2025 trade to Memphis and immediate waiver without appearing in a game; his career has since shifted to the G League and, by mid-2026, Turkey's Körfez Basket. Bust: elite, decorated college scoring production that never crossed over to consistent NBA opportunity.

name: Ousmane Dieng
notes: A French developmental prospect (Centre Fédéral, then the first European in New Zealand's Next Stars program, 12.6/5.8/2.9), genuine long-term feel and size on a young, unrefined sample. New York took him 11th (traded to Oklahoma City). Dieng needed three patient, G League-heavy seasons — a 2024 G League Finals MVP — before winning a ring in OKC's 2025 championship, then a February 2026 trade (via Charlotte and Chicago) to Milwaukee finally unlocked real production (career-high 11.0/4.6/3.6 across 30 games), earning a $17.5M re-signing. Mixed outcome: real long-term development that took years and several organizations to produce a genuine NBA role.

name: Jalen Williams
notes: A three-year Santa Clara riser who broke out as a junior (18.0 ppg on 51.3% shooting, First-Team All-WCC, the program's first draftee since Steve Nash), efficient scoring from a mid-major many teams undervalued. Oklahoma City took him 12th. Williams delivered immediately (All-Rookie First Team) and grew into a genuine superstar — a first All-Star nod, All-NBA and All-Defensive honors in 2025, a 40-point Finals Game 5 (third-youngest ever) en route to the 2025 championship — before injuries limited his 2025-26 season. Hit: a massively undervalued mid-major prospect who became a genuine All-NBA co-star and champion.

name: Jalen Duren
notes: A reclassified five-star Memphis freshman and AAC Freshman of the Year (12.0/8.1/2.1 blk), elite physical tools and rebounding on a one-year sample. Charlotte took him 13th (traded to Detroit via New York). Duren developed steadily every season with the Pistons — 9.1 up to a career-high 19.5 ppg by 2025-26 while holding 10-11 rebounds — earning his first All-Star selection and All-NBA Third Team in 2026. Hit: elite physical tools that matured into a genuine All-Star-caliber NBA center.

name: Ochai Agbaji
notes: A late-blooming Kansas senior who won Big 12 Player of the Year and NCAA Tournament Most Outstanding Player en route to a national title (18.8 ppg on 47.5/40.9% shooting, consensus First-Team All-American), elite winning production from a four-year college star. Cleveland took him 14th (traded to Utah as part of the Donovan Mitchell deal). Agbaji's production dipped in Utah (5.4-7.9 ppg) before a 2024 trade to Toronto found real growth (10.4/3.8/1.5 by 2024-25), and a further 2026 trade to Brooklyn. Mixed outcome: a real, valuable 3-and-D wing role across several teams, never quite matching his college ceiling.

name: Mark Williams
notes: Duke's ACC Defensive Player of the Year as a sophomore (11.2/7.4/2.8 blk on a Duke-record-caliber .721 FG%), elite rim protection and finishing efficiency. Charlotte took him 15th. Williams developed into a real starter (9.0 to a 15.3/10.2 2024-25 season, a 31-point game) before back injuries limited 2023-24, and a February 2025 trade to the Lakers was rescinded after he failed his physical; he was later dealt to Phoenix and re-signed for $38M in 2026. Mixed outcome: real starting-center production repeatedly complicated by health and trade uncertainty.

name: AJ Griffin
notes: A five-star McDonald's All-American whose Duke freshman season (10.4/3.9 on an elite 49.3/44.7% shooting) suggested a high offensive floor, real shooting efficiency on a limited role. Atlanta took him 16th. Griffin's strongest year came immediately (8.9 ppg as a rookie) before a sharp decline (2.4 ppg in 20 games) his second season; traded to Houston in 2024, he reached a contract buyout and announced his retirement from basketball that September to pursue full-time Christian ministry. Bust relative to his draft slot — a career cut short not by performance decline alone, but by a voluntary retirement.

name: Tari Eason
notes: A Cincinnati-to-LSU transfer who broke out as a sophomore (16.9/6.6/1.9 stl, First-Team All-SEC, SEC Sixth Man of the Year), real defensive versatility and energy production. Houston took him 17th. Eason won All-Rookie Second Team honors immediately (9.3/6.0), was limited by injury to 22 games in 2023-24, then developed into a genuine, high-value rotation piece (a career-high 12.0 ppg in 2024-25, 10.5/6.3 as a part-time starter in 2025-26), signing a five-year, $81.5M deal in 2026. Hit: real defensive energy and versatility that became a genuine, well-paid NBA rotation piece.

name: Dalen Terry
notes: Arizona's Pac-12 All-Defensive First Teamer as a sophomore starter (8.0/4.8/3.9/1.2 stl on 50.2% shooting), real playmaking and defensive versatility from a 33-4 conference-title team. Chicago took him 18th. Terry never earned consistent NBA minutes across four Bulls seasons (2.2 to a career-high 4.5 ppg), was traded and waived in a single February 2026 chain (New York to New Orleans), signed by Philadelphia before being cut for cap space, and landed with Golden State. Bust: real defensive versatility that thin offensive production never let translate into a settled NBA role.

name: Jake LaRavia
notes: An Indiana State transfer who broke out at Wake Forest (14.6/6.6/3.7, Second-Team All-ACC, a 31-point/10-rebound game against North Carolina), real all-around forward production from a mid-major path. Minnesota took him 19th (traded to Memphis). LaRavia developed gradually across three Memphis seasons (7.0 ppg) before a 2025 trade to Sacramento and a further Lakers signing ($12M) unlocked a genuine role — a full 82-game, 43-start 2025-26 season averaging 8.2/4.0/1.3 stl. Solid outcome: steady, patient development into a real NBA rotation contributor.

name: Malaki Branham
notes: Ohio State's Big Ten Freshman of the Year (13.7/3.6/2.0 on 49.8/41.6% shooting, a 35-point outburst against Nebraska), efficient scoring on a one-and-done sample. San Antonio took him 20th. Branham's rookie year showed real promise (10.2 ppg, 32 starts) before a steady decline (9.2, then 5.0 ppg) led to a 2025 trade to Washington, a further 2026 trade to Charlotte and immediate waiver, and a G League stint before an Exhibit 10 deal with Orlando in September 2026. Bust: an efficient rookie debut that never sustained into a lasting NBA role.

name: Christian Braun
notes: Kansas's Second-Team All-Big 12 junior (a 1,000-point scorer, a game-sealing defensive stop and 12/12 in the 2022 title game), real winning production and energy from a champion. Denver took him 21st. Braun won a title as a rookie in a bench role (the fifth player ever with consecutive NCAA and NBA championships), grew every season (4.7 to 7.3 to a career-high 15.4/5.2/2.6 in 2024-25), and signed a $125M extension in 2025 before a November ankle sprain sidelined him. Hit: real winning production and energy that developed into a genuine NBA starter and two-time champion.

name: Walker Kessler
notes: Auburn's SEC Defensive Player of the Year and Third-Team All-American as a freshman (a school single-season and national blocks record, an 11-block triple-double against LSU), elite, ready-made rim protection. Memphis took him 22nd (traded to Minnesota, then Utah as part of the Rudy Gobert deal). Kessler won All-Rookie First Team honors immediately (9.2/8.4/2.3 blk) and developed into a genuine double-double force (11.1/12.2/2.4 blk, a 25-rebound game) before shoulder surgery cut short 2025-26; he signed a $130M sign-and-trade deal with the Lakers in 2026. Hit: elite college shot-blocking that became a genuine starting-caliber NBA center.

name: David Roddy
notes: Colorado State's two-time First-Team All-Mountain West Player of the Year (19.2/7.5/2.9 on 57.1/43.8% shooting), an efficient, positionless combo forward from a mid-major. Philadelphia took him 23rd (on behalf of Memphis). Roddy carved out real early Grizzlies rotation minutes (6.7 to 8.4 ppg) before a 2024 trade to Phoenix, then a well-traveled run through Atlanta, Philadelphia, Houston, Toronto and Denver on short-term deals, before a 2026 signing with Israel's Hapoel Jerusalem. Bust: real efficient college scoring that never found a settled long-term NBA home.

name: MarJon Beauchamp
notes: An unconventional prospect who starred at a junior college (30.7/10.5/4.8 in 12 games) before choosing G League Ignite over a Division I transfer, real athletic scoring upside from a nontraditional path. Milwaukee took him 24th. Beauchamp's production peaked early (a 20-point game as a rookie) before a steady decline to marginal Bucks minutes, trades to the Clippers and Knicks, and a 2025 Philadelphia two-way stint after strong G League play; by 2026 his career shifted to Germany's Bayern Munich. Bust: real athletic tools that never found a settled, lasting NBA rotation spot.

name: Blake Wesley
notes: A one-and-done Notre Dame freshman and Second-Team All-ACC guard (14.4/3.7/2.4), real shot-creation burst on a thin sample. San Antonio took him 25th. A torn MCL derailed his rookie season early, and over three Spurs seasons his role and efficiency steadily declined (5.0 to 4.3 ppg on weak shooting splits) before a 2025 trade to Washington, a waiver, and a Portland signing — a fifth metatarsal fracture in late 2025 requiring surgery. Bust: real athletic guard tools repeatedly undercut by injury and a shrinking role.

name: Wendell Moore Jr.
notes: Duke's Second-Team All-ACC junior and Julius Erving Award winner (10.7/4.9 career, a 19-10-10 triple-double against Army, North Carolina Mr. Basketball), real winning-program versatility. Dallas took him 26th (traded to Houston, then Minnesota). Moore never found consistent NBA minutes (mostly G League time with Minnesota) across stints with Detroit, Charlotte and Boston/Detroit again, before a 2026 move to Italy's Virtus Bologna (career NBA: 2.3 ppg over 96 games). Bust: real college versatility that never crossed over to a real NBA rotation role.

name: Nikola Jović
notes: A Serbian big-wing prospect (Mega Basket) who torched the EuroLeague Next Generation Tournament (29.3/10.3/4.5/1.8 blk) and earned ABA League Top Prospect honors, elite feel and production against elite European youth competition. Miami took him 27th. Jović played a rotation role immediately (including the 2023 Finals loss to Denver), then developed steadily every season (7.7 to 10.7 ppg by 2024-25), earning a $62.4M extension in 2025. Solid outcome: real, patient development into a genuine, valuable Heat rotation forward.

name: Patrick Baldwin Jr.
notes: A consensus five-star, top-ranked 2021 recruit whose lone Milwaukee season (his father's program) was cut to 11 games by leg and ankle injuries (12.1/5.8 in that span), real talent on a badly injury-shortened, unverifiable sample. Golden State took him 28th. Baldwin never found NBA traction (3.7 ppg as a rookie, mostly G League time) across stints with Washington, the Clippers, Philadelphia and Sacramento, before a 2026 signing with Serbia's Crvena zvezda. Bust: real recruiting-era talent that an injury-wrecked lone college season never let the NBA properly evaluate or develop.

name: TyTy Washington Jr.
notes: A five-star Kentucky point guard who broke John Wall's single-game assist record (12.5/4.5/3.9, Second-Team All-SEC), elite pure playmaking on a one-and-done sample. Memphis took him 29th (traded to Minnesota, then Houston). Washington never earned real NBA minutes (4.7 ppg as a rookie, declining further through Milwaukee, Phoenix and the Clippers on two-way deals) before a 2026 move to France's ASVEL Lyon-Villeurbanne. Bust: elite college playmaking pedigree that never crossed over to consistent NBA opportunity.

name: Peyton Watson
notes: A five-star, highest-ranked-in-California recruit whose UCLA freshman role stayed minimal (3.3/2.9 on 32.2% FG, an intentional one-and-done situation), pure long-term athletic upside on almost no real production. Oklahoma City took him 30th (traded to Denver). Watson won a championship as a rookie in a reserve role, developed steadily (6.7 to 8.1 ppg) before a full 2025-26 breakout (14.6/4.9/2.1, four 30-point games, a Western Conference Player of the Week award, sitting out the playoffs for free agency protection), then signed an $88M deal with Cleveland in 2026. Hit: a near-zero-production recruit whose patient developmental bet became a genuine breakout NBA starter and champion.

name: Andrew Nembhard
notes: A Florida-to-Gonzaga transfer who developed into a First-Team All-WCC senior floor general (11.8/5.8, an elite assist-to-turnover ratio), real winning-program point-guard feel. Indiana took him 31st, signing the largest rookie deal ever given a second-rounder. Nembhard started immediately (9.5/4.5) and grew every season — a 2023 Rising Star, then a 2025-26 breakout to 16.9/7.7 as Indiana's full-time starter — signing a $59M extension in 2024. Hit: a massively undervalued second-round transfer who became a genuine starting NBA point guard.

name: Caleb Houstan
notes: A five-star, reclassified McDonald's All-American on Michigan's No. 1-ranked recruiting class, whose lone college season underwhelmed on efficiency (10.1 ppg on 38.4/35.5% shooting), real shooting-specialist upside on a disappointing sample. Orlando took him 32nd. Houstan settled into marginal Magic rotation minutes (3.8-4.3 ppg) with steadily improving three-point shooting (reaching 40%) before a 2025 move to Atlanta (waived) and a 2026 signing with New Orleans. Bust: elite recruiting pedigree that thin college production and thin NBA opportunity never let fully develop.

name: Christian Koloko
notes: Arizona's Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Year and Most Improved Player as a junior (12.6/7.3/2.8 blk, a 22-point/4-block tournament MVP game), elite defensive anchor upside. Toronto took him 33rd. A promising rookie season (3.1 ppg, 58 games) was upended by a blood clot in April 2023 that required a fitness-to-play clearance process; waived by Toronto in 2024, Koloko has since bounced through the Lakers, Grizzlies, Hawks and Pelicans via two-way and hardship deals. Mixed outcome: real defensive tools whose career has been defined as much by a serious health scare as by on-court production.

name: Jaylin Williams
notes: Arkansas's First-Team All-SEC sophomore (10.9/9.8, an NCAA-leading 54 charges drawn, a school single-season rebounding record), elite hustle and rebounding feel. Oklahoma City took him 34th, the first NBA player of Vietnamese descent. Williams settled into a genuine role-playing rotation spot alongside similarly-named teammate Jalen Williams (5.9-5.9 ppg, two career triple-doubles), won the 2025 championship over Indiana, and signed a $24M extension. Solid outcome: real hustle-and-rebounding translation into a valuable NBA role and championship.

name: Max Christie
notes: A five-star Michigan State freshman and Big Ten All-Freshman honoree (9.3/3.5 on modest 38.2/31.7% shooting), real shooting-guard upside on an inefficient one-year sample. The Lakers took him 35th. Christie developed patiently (3.1 to 4.2 to a real 8.5 ppg breakout in 2024-25, an In-Season Tournament title) before a 2025 blockbuster trade to Dallas (part of the Luka Dončić deal) fully unlocked him — 12.3 ppg on 40.4% three-point shooting across every game in 2025-26. Hit: patient development that became a genuine, efficient NBA starter after a change of scenery.

name: Gabriele Procida
notes: An Italian prospect who turned pro at 17 and became one of the youngest players ever to score 24 points in a league game, real long-term shooting-guard upside from a young age. Portland took him 36th (traded to Detroit, later to Utah) but he never signed, developing instead through Fortitudo Bologna and Alba Berlin — winning the 2023-24 EuroLeague Rising Star award (8.3/1.4 stl) — before a 2025 move to Real Madrid. Never played in the NBA — a real, still-developing EuroLeague talent instead.

name: Jaden Hardy
notes: A five-star G League Ignite product (17.7/4.6/3.2 on 35.1% FG), elite scoring upside on inefficient shooting from a non-college path. Sacramento took him 37th (traded to Dallas). Hardy settled into a real, steady Mavericks bench-scoring role (6.9-8.8 ppg across four seasons) and reached the 2024 Finals, signing an $18M extension in 2024; a 2026 trade to Washington produced a career-high 12.6 ppg stretch before a further trade (part of the Deandre Ayton deal) sent him to the Lakers. Solid outcome: real, efficient bench scoring that has held a genuine NBA role for four-plus seasons.

name: Kennedy Chandler
notes: A one-and-done Tennessee point guard and Second-Team All-SEC honoree (13.9/4.7/2.2 stl), a projected top-20 talent who fell to the late first round. San Antonio took him 38th (traded to Memphis). Chandler's rookie chance stayed marginal (2.2 ppg, waived in 2023) and he spent two-plus years in the G League before a strong 2025-26 flash on 10-day deals with Utah (15.0/6.7/3.4, a 31-point game). Bust relative to his college billing, though real signs of NBA-caliber guard play have finally emerged.

name: Khalifa Diop
notes: A 7'1" Senegalese center who developed through Spain's Gran Canaria academy, earning EuroCup Rising Star honors and multiple ACB All-Young Players selections, a genuine long-term draft-and-stash rim-protecting prospect. Cleveland took him 39th and stashed him in Europe for four years — a EuroCup title with Baskonia — before finally signing him to an NBA contract in September 2026. Never played in the NBA as of this writing — a real, patiently-developed European center about to get his first NBA chance.

name: Bryce McGowens
notes: Nebraska's highest-ranked recruit ever and Third-Team All-Big Ten freshman (16.8/5.2/1.4), real scoring instincts from a one-and-done season. Minnesota took him 40th (traded to Charlotte). McGowens settled into marginal minutes (5.2 ppg across two Hornets seasons) before a difficult Portland stint (a season-ending rib fracture in the G League) and a 2025 New Orleans two-way deal that converted to a standard $6.2M contract in 2026. Bust relative to his high school pedigree, though a real, sustained NBA roster spot has finally taken hold.

name: E.J. Liddell
notes: Ohio State's Third-Team All-American junior and First-Team All-Big Ten forward (19.4/7.9/2.5/2.6 blk, a 34-point game), elite, versatile college production. New Orleans took him 41st. A torn ACL suffered in Summer League play derailed his rookie season entirely, and Liddell has since bounced through New Orleans, Chicago and Brooklyn on modest deals, showing real flashes late (a 21-point game with Brooklyn in 2025-26) before a 2026 move to Greece's Aris Thessaloniki. Bust: elite college production whose NBA start was wiped out by injury before it began.

name: Trevor Keels
notes: A five-star, top shooting-guard recruit whose lone Duke season showed real scoring punch (11.5/3.4/2.7, ACC All-Rookie, a 25-point debut against Kentucky) on an inefficient profile. New York took him 42nd. Keels's NBA chance stayed minimal (3 games as a Knick) before two-plus G League seasons, including a record-setting 12-for-12 three-point, 46-point game in 2026, that finally earned a Miami two-way deal. Bust relative to his recruiting pedigree, though real, recently-validated shooting talent has kept a path to the NBA open.

name: Moussa Diabaté
notes: A five-star Michigan freshman (9.0/6.0 on an elite 54.2% FG, Big Ten All-Freshman), real rim-running and rebounding tools on a limited offensive role. LA Clippers took him 43rd. Diabaté needed patient two-way G League seasoning (a G League All-Rookie season with 20-20 games) before a 2024 Charlotte signing (standard deal by 2025) unlocked a genuine breakout — 7.9/8.7 on 63.1% shooting across 73 games (47 starts) in 2025-26. Hit: real energy-big tools that steadily developed into a genuine NBA starting-caliber role.

name: Ryan Rollins
notes: Toledo's First-Team All-MAC sophomore breakout (18.9/6.0/3.6, a 35-point tournament finale), real scoring and playmaking production from a mid-major. Atlanta took him 44th (traded to Golden State). A Jones fracture wiped out most of his rookie year, and a 2023 trade to Washington (part of the Jordan Poole deal) led to a quick waiver before Milwaukee's two-way signing finally found him a home — a real 2024-25 role (6.2 ppg) exploding into a 2025-26 starting job (17.3/5.6, a 32-point game), earning a $12M deal. Hit: real mid-major scoring talent that patient development turned into a genuine breakout starter.

name: Josh Minott
notes: A four-star Memphis recruit whose lone college season stayed limited in minutes (6.6/3.8 in 14.6 mpg, AAC All-Freshman), real long-term athletic upside on a thin sample. Charlotte took him 45th (traded to Minnesota). Minott's Wolves tenure produced marginal bench minutes (2.4 ppg over three seasons) before a 2025 Boston signing expanded his role (5.8 ppg), and a further 2026 trade to Brooklyn finally unlocked real production (a 24-point game, 10.8 ppg), earning a $9M re-signing. Solid outcome: real athletic tools that took several organizations and years to find a genuine NBA role.

name: Ismael Kamagate
notes: A French center (Paris Basketball) who was LNB Pro A's Best Defender and Domestic Player of the Year in 2022, considered a possible first-round talent who instead stayed overseas. Detroit took him 46th, his rights traded repeatedly (Portland, Denver, the Clippers, and by 2026 Cleveland) without him ever signing. Kamagate has instead built a genuine, accomplished European career — EuroCup blocks leader, a 2025 EuroLeague All-First Team season with Olimpia Milano. Never played in the NBA — a real, high-level EuroLeague center instead.

name: Vince Williams Jr.
notes: A four-year VCU wing who overcame multiple shoulder injuries to become a First-Team All-Atlantic 10 senior (14.1/6.0/3.0), real well-rounded production from a mid-major program. Memphis took him 47th. Williams developed into a genuine Grizzlies rotation piece — a real 2023-24 breakout (10.0/5.6/3.4 across 33 starts) — before a 2026 trade to Utah (part of the Jaren Jackson Jr. deal) was followed almost immediately by a season-ending torn ACL. Mixed outcome: real, multi-year NBA rotation production interrupted by a serious late-career injury.

name: Kendall Brown
notes: A five-star Baylor recruit and the program's highest-ranked signee in a decade, whose lone college season showed elite finishing efficiency (9.7/4.9 on 58.4% FG) but limited shot creation. Minnesota took him 48th (traded to Indiana). A tibia stress fracture requiring surgery wiped out most of his early Pacers tenure (21 games, 1.4 ppg across two seasons) before a 2024 waiver, and Brown has since cycled through the Nets' and Celtics' G League affiliates. Bust: real athletic finishing tools that a serious leg injury never let develop into NBA opportunity.

name: Isaiah Mobley
notes: A five-star recruit and USC's First-Team All-Pac-12 junior (14.2/8.3 on 46/36% shooting), real stretch-four production from a three-year college star (brother of Evan Mobley). Cleveland took him 49th. Mobley's NBA chance stayed almost entirely in the G League (18.6/8.1 with Cleveland's affiliate, 17.5/7.9 with Philadelphia's) — only 23 total NBA games (2.6 ppg) — before his career shifted to Turkey and, by 2025, Israel's Hapoel Jerusalem. Bust: real, winning college production that a crowded NBA path never let past G League depth.

name: Matteo Spagnolo
notes: An Italian guard who became the first Italian in Real Madrid's youth academy and made his senior debut at 18, real long-term guard upside from a top European pedigree. Minnesota took him 50th but he never signed, instead developing through loan spells (Vanoli Cremona, Trento) and a three-year Alba Berlin deal (7.3/3.4 in EuroLeague) before a 2025 move to Saski Baskonia through 2028; his draft rights moved to Charlotte in 2026. Never played in the NBA — a real, still-developing EuroLeague guard instead.

name: Tyrese Martin
notes: A Rhode Island-to-UConn transfer who developed into a real four-year producer (13.6/7.5 as a senior, 1,000 career points, a 25-point game against Marquette), well-rounded wing-forward production from two mid-major-to-high-major stops. Golden State took him 51st (traded to Atlanta). Martin's NBA chance stayed marginal for years (heavy G League time, a real 18.1 ppg G League season) before a 2024 Brooklyn signing produced genuine flashes (a 30-point game, 8.7 ppg across 60 games in 2024-25) before a 2026 waiver and Philadelphia stint; he signed with FC Barcelona in mid-2026. Mixed outcome: real, if brief, NBA rotation production before a move to Europe.

name: Karlo Matković
notes: A Croatian big man who developed through Cedevita, OKK Beograd and Mega Basket, real long-term stretch-four upside from a proven European pedigree. New Orleans took him 52nd and stashed him overseas — a EuroCup blocks title with Cedevita Olimpija — before signing him in 2024. Matković has since become a genuine Pelicans rotation piece, appearing in 104 games at 6.5/4.2 on an efficient 58.9% shooting through 2025-26. Solid outcome: a patient draft-and-stash bet that became a real, efficient NBA rotation big.

name: JD Davison
notes: A five-star Alabama recruit, the program's first under Nate Oats, whose lone college season showed real playmaking feel (8.5/4.8/4.3, SEC All-Freshman). Boston took him 53rd. Davison's NBA minutes stayed minimal (2.1 ppg over four seasons) but he won a 2024 championship in a bench role and was G League MVP in 2025 (25.1/5.2/7.5 with Maine), before stints with Houston and, by September 2026, an Exhibit 10 deal with Orlando. Bust relative to his recruiting hype at the NBA level, though a genuine G League star and NBA champion.

name: Yannick Nzosa
notes: A Congolese center who made his Liga ACB debut at 16 (ACB All-Young Players honors) before a five-month athletic pubalgia injury dropped his draft stock from top-five buzz to the late second round. Washington took him 54th but he never signed, remaining with Unicaja Málaga through a string of Spanish-league loans (Real Betis, Estudiantes, Fuenlabrada, San Pablo Burgos) before returning to Unicaja in 2026. Never played in the NBA — real, once-elite pre-injury upside that has instead built a modest Spanish-league career.

name: Gui Santos
notes: A Brazilian wing who turned pro at 16 with Minas Tênis Clube and earned NBB Sixth Man of the Year (10.1/5.1) before a 2021 Nike Hoop Summit World Team selection, real long-term international upside. Golden State took him 55th and developed him patiently through the G League before a 2023 signing. Santos grew every season (3.6 to 4.1 to a 9.2 ppg 2025-26 breakout, a 31-point game, a $15M extension) as a real rotation piece on a title contender. Hit: patient draft-and-develop that produced a genuine, growing NBA role.

name: Luke Travers
notes: An Australian NBL prospect (Perth Wildcats, a 2020 NBL championship, SBL Most Improved Player) who chose the pro path over U.S. college offers, real athletic versatility from a winning program. Cleveland took him 56th. Travers needed two years of additional NBL development (Melbourne United, 12.4/7.6) before a 2024 two-way signing produced brief NBA minutes (1.7 ppg across 24 games over two seasons) before a February 2026 waiver (to clear space for Dennis Schröder and Keon Ellis) sent him back to Melbourne United. Bust at the NBA level, a real NBL contributor throughout.

name: Jabari Walker
notes: Colorado's First-Team All-Pac-12 sophomore breakout (14.6/9.4 on 33 starts), real rebounding and floor-stretching production. Portland took him 57th. Walker developed into a genuine rotation piece by his second year (a career-high 8.9/7.1 in 2023-24) before a decline and G League assignment in 2024-25, then a 2025 Philadelphia two-way deal converted to a standard contract in 2026 (4.3/3.0 across 64 games). Solid outcome: real, if inconsistent, NBA rotation-big production across two organizations.

name: Hugo Besson
notes: A French guard who led France's second-tier league in scoring (19.5 ppg with Saint-Quentin) before a solid New Zealand NBL season (13.9 ppg), a top-40 draft prospect by ESPN's ranking. Indiana took him 58th, the draft's final pick (traded to Milwaukee, later to New York). Besson never signed, instead playing through a hip injury with Metropolitans 92 and bouncing through Serbia's FMP, Italy's Varese and Turkish clubs Manisa and Tofaş before a 2026 signing with ASVEL Lyon-Villeurbanne. Never played in the NBA — Mr. Irrelevant-adjacent draft slot, a real if well-traveled European scoring career instead.
